nodes.label: Content Partners Custom Zoho Module (P0-OPS-05)
nodes.rationale: Module shell was human click-work (Zoho CRM has no public create-module API — a permanent split), the eleven §6.2 fields were API work, all verified by metadata read-back. Organization module (not team) so sales staff can see records; default Email/record-image layout items stripped per §6.4. Mapper facts: Zoho prepends -None- to every picklist (omit rather than send), mandatory is a layout property unenforceable via API, removing a field from layout does not delete it.

nodes.label: SponsorX_ID External Field on Five Zoho Modules (P0-OPS-06)
nodes.norm_label: sponsorx_id external field on five zoho modules (p0-ops-06)
nodes.rationale: Closed gap G-1: SponsorX_ID text(50) external field created and verified on Accounts, Contacts, Leads, Deals, Tasks. Zoho lessons: uniqueness is case-insensitive only (never case-normalise ids), unique cannot combine with external (external is inherently unique), field labels cap at 25 chars and derive the api_name. Built in production because sandbox creation is UI-only and the OAuth token is production-scoped; a later sandbox inherits the work.

nodes.label: Zoho Credentials & Sandbox Spec (P0-OPS-04)
nodes.rationale: OAuth scope list derived from the object register, not defaulted: no DELETE scope on any module and never ZohoCRM.modules.ALL, because the mapping suspends records and never deletes. Books scopes deferred until O-1 closes. Token rules: cache and refresh on expiry (Zoho caps refresh-token issuance), record who authorised (token dies with their account); domains are part of the data-residency answer (US DC).

nodes.label: SponsorX Zoho Field Mapping Document (P0-PMO-08)
nodes.rationale: v0.2: all nine §18 objects mapped field-by-field with direction and system-of-record per field, verified against the live iCARRe Foundation org metadata (103 field API names, 26 picklist values, 0 missing). Key findings: no external-ID field existed (gap G-1), Campaign maps to Deals not the stock Campaigns module, only 3 of 8 AthleteState values ever reach Zoho, nine Prisma schema gaps handed to P3-BE-01.

nodes.label: Cloudflare R2
nodes.rationale: Video on app-server disk is a bad idea; R2 solves a problem that costs real time to solve in-house. Kept from the original stack.

nodes.label: PDF Worker (Unconfirmed Requirement)
nodes.rationale: Addendum A10: PDF generation appears nowhere in the blueprint's 39 sections, yet the worker shaped the original hosting architecture. Confirm the requirement is real before it shapes any more; if real, headless Chromium in a Railway container is what leaving Vercel bought.

nodes.label: Railway
nodes.rationale: App + PDF worker + Postgres in one project over private networking: one deploy, one dashboard, one place for env vars. Removes Vercel's function-duration constraint that originally forced the worker split.

nodes.label: Transactional Email Vendor (Undecided)
nodes.rationale: Addendum A1: §27 lists it and the §39 loop does not run without it — invitations, acceptance requests, deadlines, revision requests, approvals are all email. Resend / Postmark / SES; pick when the first notification is built, keep it reversible behind a single send interface. SMS stays out of Phase 1.

nodes.label: Zoho (CRM + Books)
nodes.rationale: A business tool the team already uses daily; stays exactly where the blueprint put it — behind the queue. If Zoho is down, sponsors still browse, athletes still accept orders, fans still redeem.

nodes.label: Phase 1 Open Decisions
nodes.rationale: Do not code around silently: Phase 1 payment policy (§37 gate one, expected earnings-status-only, no tax ID), data residency (since decided US East), guardian e-signature for minors (legal question), transactional email provider, and whether the PDF worker has a real requirement.

nodes.label: §39 Protected Core Loop
nodes.rationale: athlete application → approval → NIL job/rate → sponsor brief → matching → invitation → Campaign Order → deliverable → tracking/reward → earnings → sponsor report. When scope must give, cut from the self-service ecommerce end, never from this loop.

nodes.label: SponsorX Phase 1 — Managed Marketplace
nodes.rationale: Phase 1 is a managed marketplace: sponsors browse and submit briefs, BTG staff does matching, pricing, conflict checks and invoicing. No self-service checkout — that is Phase 2. Scope, not stack, is the binding constraint (two people vs §31's 4.5–7.5 FTE); cut from the ecommerce end, never from the §39 loop.

nodes.label: Transactional Outbox + pg-boss
nodes.rationale: outbox.ts provides transactional enqueue; the worker boots pg-boss (queues live in our Postgres, migrations run on worker boot) and drains the outbox — so a domain write and its side-effect job commit atomically.

nodes.label: R2 Two-Bucket Presign Pattern
nodes.rationale: Presigned PUT/GET via @aws-sdk against two buckets (public CDN vs private signed) plus image derivatives on the worker without next/image — implementing Addendum A8 while staying host-portable.

nodes.label: Repo Layout — One Repo, Two Deployables
nodes.norm_label: repo layout — one repo, two deployables
nodes.rationale: Next app + worker as two services in one Railway project over private networking, both importing src/server so a job and a route handler can never disagree. Not a monorepo: two package.json files would mean two lockfiles drifting apart on the code that decides how much an athlete gets paid. Contracts are Zod schemas in src/contracts feeding OpenAPI generation.

nodes.label: A-Gates · Resolve the Open Decisions
nodes.rationale: Six written decisions run in parallel with A0–A3 and block Block B, not Block A: payment policy (§37 gate one), data residency, guardian e-signature, email provider, SMS deferral, counsel-approved Campaign Order and Content Collaboration Agreement templates.

nodes.label: B0 · Foundations
nodes.rationale: The heaviest milestone, unblocks everything: pins & deps, full Prisma schema + migrations + partial indexes, Railway web/worker/postgres project, Clerk replacing mock-auth with requireActor(), actor.ts + scope.ts + authz matrix green in CI, outbox + pg-boss, R2 two-bucket presign, contracts registry → openapi.json, seed job, lint rule failing bare findMany().

nodes.label: Data Residency — US East (Decided)
nodes.rationale: Addendum A7, resolved 2026-09-11: US-only confirmed (NIL is a US legal construct, USD pricing, high-school athletes). Region is East, not West — prelaunch materials target the DMV and Baltimore, org number is a 443 area code. Railway us-east4-eqdc4a (Virginia) + R2 location hint ENAM, both fixed at resource creation; gates P0-OPS-02 and P2-OPS-01. Note: Zoho org timezone is PST, contradicting a DMV operation.

nodes.label: No Tax ID Storage in Phase 1
nodes.norm_label: no tax id storage in phase 1
nodes.rationale: Addendum A6: §11 asks only for payment recipient and onboarding status, §26 forbids raw bank credentials, §27 makes Phase 1 payments invoice/reference tracking only, payout_accounts arrives in Phase 2. If Phase 1 tracks earnings status while money moves outside the system, no tax ID is collected and no restricted store is needed — but the written payment policy §37 requires must say so.

nodes.label: One Thing to Operate
nodes.rationale: Team size is two people; the real cost was two deploy paths (Vercel + Railway), not six vendors. Configure-once services (Neon, R2, Clerk) carry near-zero ongoing work, so the goal is one thing to operate, not one vendor. Six vendors down to four (five with email); two deploy paths down to one.

nodes.label: Portability Rules
nodes.rationale: Keep the hosting decision reversible: Next.js output 'standalone' (ordinary Node server), treat ISR / next/image optimization / edge middleware as host-specific primitives adopted deliberately, and never call Zoho inline from a request path.

nodes.label: Postgres Job Queue (Redis Deferred)
nodes.rationale: Addendum A3: Phase 1 volume is tens to low hundreds of jobs/day; SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED against Railway Postgres delivers §27's durability with orders of magnitude of headroom. A deliberate, recorded deviation from §27; revisit on sustained queue depth/latency.

nodes.label: R2 Two Access Patterns
nodes.rationale: Addendum A8: public CDN video and §26's signed private storage for agreements/creative assets must not share a bucket policy — same vendor, two configurations. Athlete uploads go direct to R2 via presigned URLs, never through the app server (phone-shot video through a Node request path becomes an outage).

nodes.label: Zoho Bi-directional Sync (Four Objects)
nodes.rationale: Addendum A9: §18 makes Accounts, Contacts, Deals, Tasks bi-directional and flows Invoice/Payment Reference from Zoho Books. Outbound is fully queued; inbound Zoho webhooks land in the queue too, never in a request path that blocks on Zoho. External IDs on both sides prevent duplicates; webhook_deliveries records inbound attempts.

nodes.label: Zoho Boundary
nodes.rationale: Zoho knows who you're selling to and whether they've paid; SponsorX knows what was promised, who's delivering it and whether it worked. Keep Zoho, don't build on Zoho: Creator and Catalyst were rejected because both extend the Zoho ecosystem rather than host a public consumer product, and Deluge/Catalyst is a far smaller talent pool than Next.js.

nodes.label: Zoho Boundary (Architecture Rule)
nodes.rationale: Zoho knows who we're selling to and whether they've paid; SponsorX knows what was promised, who's delivering it and whether it worked. Keep Zoho, don't build on Zoho; Zoho never touches a request path — all exchanges queued through the worker.

nodes.label: INFINEX World API Architecture (v1)
nodes.rationale: INFINEX consumes SponsorX as sponsorship system-of-record; virtual impressions require rendered placement, on-screen threshold and dwell time, with server-signed events for monetized metrics.

nodes.label: RBAC + Tenant Scoping Permission Model
nodes.rationale: Every protected record includes tenant_id; sensitive actions require explicit permissions rather than role names alone; all administrative mutations write an audit_log record.

nodes.label: Zoho CRM Integration (v1 Spec)
nodes.rationale: SponsorX is system-of-record for inventory/campaign delivery, Zoho for sales relationship; event queue with retries and external IDs so Zoho outages never break campaign operations.

nodes.label: Commerce Attribution Framework (Pluggable Methodology)
nodes.rationale: Attribution treated as a pluggable methodology, not universal truth; deterministic match attempted first, probabilistic methods explicitly marked with confidence/method metadata.

nodes.label: Commission & Payout Ledger (Immutable Financial Snapshot)
nodes.rationale: Order gross revenue converted into a versioned ledger at contract time rather than calculated ad hoc at payout; historical closed payouts never recalculated when a future commission rule changes.

nodes.label: Phase 2 - Marketplace & Athlete Commerce
nodes.rationale: External property onboarding, listings, cart/reservation/checkout, commission engine, payout orchestration and wallet rewards; BTG retains governance, floor pricing and dispute handling.

nodes.label: Phase 3 - Intelligence & Attribution
nodes.rationale: Launch with rules/statistical models before ML; every recommendation exposes model version, confidence and factor breakdown; estimated revenue is never labeled verified.

nodes.label: Phase 4 - INFINEX World Integration
nodes.rationale: SponsorX remains commercial/reporting system-of-record; INFINEX is an activation client that renders placements and returns verified interaction events; virtual impressions withheld from sponsors until viewability and de-duplication are validated.

nodes.label: Transactional Outbox + Idempotent Integration Pattern
nodes.rationale: Domain writes and to-be-synced events commit in the same transaction, a worker drains the outbox with idempotency keys, backoff and dead-letter - preventing Zoho/SponsorX drift and double-writes.

nodes.label: Environments and Deploy Pipeline
nodes.rationale: DATABASE_URL Neon pooled for web, DIRECT_URL for worker and migrations (pooled connections break advisory locks during migration). Zoho credentials worker-only — the web app never calls Zoho directly. Migrations run as a release step against DIRECT_URL, never in the build (a Vercel build that migrates will migrate once per preview deploy). Worker deploys before web on any release adding a job type. Three environments: preview (shared Neon branch, seeded fake data), staging (pilot cohort UAT), production (point-in-time restore). Never seed production from the pilot spreadsheet by hand — write the importer as a job. Vercel function limits: report rendering, bulk imports and Zoho backfills are worker jobs; if you find yourself raising a route's maxDuration, the work is in the wrong place. Own the short-link domain, no third-party shortener.

nodes.label: Prisma Schema (Core Tables)
nodes.rationale: Four conventions run through every model: tenantId on everything, state enums lifted verbatim from §21, external IDs plus a sync-origin marker on anything Zoho touches, and events stored as rows rather than counters. Models: Tenant, User (clerkId mirror — identity lives in Clerk), Athlete (slug public URL, birthDate drives guardian path), AthleteSocial, NilJob (SX-01..SX-07), AthleteRate (versioned, cents), Sponsor, Campaign, CampaignOrder, Deliverable, CreativeAsset (r2Key, signed-URL access only), MetricDaily, TrackingLink, Reward, RewardToken (opaque token, never the record id), RewardEvent, Earning (taxYear index for year-end rollup), Agreement (bodyHash sha256 of exact text shown), AgreementAcceptance, OutboxJob, AuditLog.

nodes.label: Athlete Value Proposition
nodes.rationale: Paid for content you are half-making already; you pick each job — nothing is automatic and you can say no with no penalty; not exclusive — your own deals stay yours, this is not signing your career over to an agency; under 18 requires a parent or guardian to approve before anything happens; you can see what you have earned and exactly where it stands.

nodes.label: Five-Step Campaign Flow
nodes.rationale: 1) Business states goal and budget. 2) SponsorX picks athletes from the roster — matched to neighbourhood and customers, not by follower count but by who actually gets engagement and reliably delivers. 3) Athletes make content; the sponsor approves everything before it goes public. 4) Fans get an offer: each athlete gets their own code; a fan scans, claims, and redeems in-store. 5) The business gets the numbers — views, engagement, scans, claims, redemptions — per athlete, so they know who moved the needle.

nodes.label: Sponsor Objection Handling
nodes.rationale: Four expected objections: price — start at $750, three athletes, one post each, a real report, deliberately cheap enough to say yes without a meeting; 'just influencer marketing?' — no, influencers rent an audience, athletes rent standing in a community (a kid people watch play on Friday night carries weight a random creator does not); proof — in-store redemption, not impressions; brand risk — the sponsor approves every piece before publication.

nodes.label: Cloudflare R2 File Storage
nodes.rationale: Files live on R2, outside the web host, because athlete video doesn't belong in a web host. Implementation guide: bucket is private, all access via signed URLs; creative assets store an r2Key.

nodes.label: One Postgres, Run by Neon
nodes.rationale: Every record in the product, plus the job queue and the audit log. Notably NOT in it: passwords (Clerk), files (R2), invoices (Zoho), bank details (nowhere — §26 forbids it), and tax IDs, which need a restricted store to be decided before athlete one.

nodes.label: Background Worker on Railway
nodes.rationale: Sits outside the web host on purpose because Vercel kills long-running requests, and a 12-page PDF render is exactly that. All Zoho exchanges cross through this worker, queued.

nodes.label: Vercel Hosting
nodes.rationale: One deployment serves everything a person looks at: the marketing site, all 12 screens, all three portals, the fan QR page. Push to GitHub, Vercel builds it, it's live. (Hosting choice later superseded by Railway per the repo's stack-decision.md.)

nodes.label: Authorization Test Matrix
nodes.rationale: §30 acceptance criterion — not a checklist item at the end but a generated test that runs on every commit. Seed two tenants, two sponsors and two athletes, then assert every role against every resource (e.g. SPONSOR_ADMIN denied athleteRate.amount, ATHLETE denied campaign.budget, GUARDIAN allowed ward's campaignOrder). Add a row every time you add a resource; when someone widens a scope function to fix a bug, this suite tells them what else they just widened.

nodes.label: Vertical Slice Build Order
nodes.rationale: Every vertical slice lands in the same sequence: 1) Zod contract (the schema is the specification), 2) Prisma model and migration, 3) scope function plus its authorization-matrix rows, 4) domain function with audit and outbox calls, 5) thin route handler or server action, 6) UI, 7) E2E test. Steps 1-4 are where the product lives. If a rule about who can see what exists only in a React component, it is not a rule — it is a suggestion the API will happily ignore. Deviating is how you end up with a UI that cannot be secured.

nodes.label: Pinned Package Versions
nodes.rationale: Pin exactly, no carets, for the first two sprints: a pod of three across time zones does not need a transitive minor bump breaking the build on a Tuesday. Move to ranges once CI is trustworthy. Key pins: next 16.3.4 (params is a Promise), react 19.2.8, prisma 7.10.0 (not 8.x release-candidate; prisma.config.ts + explicit generated-client output), @clerk/nextjs (orgs map to tenants, custom session claims carry role), pg-boss (queues in Postgres, migrations on worker boot), tailwindcss (CSS-first, no tailwind.config.js), zod 4.5.4, playwright (E2E tests plus PDF rendering on worker).

nodes.label: Repo Layout (One Repository, Two Deployables)
nodes.rationale: One repository, two deployables (Next app + worker), both importing from src/server so a job and a route handler can never disagree about what a Campaign Order is. Why not a monorepo: Turborepo earns its keep only with separate deploy artifacts and different dependency trees; here the worker imports the same Prisma client and domain functions, and two package.json files would mean two lockfiles drifting apart on the code that decides how much an athlete gets paid. Key paths: src/app/(public), r/[token] fan redeem (server-rendered, no JS), t/[code] tracking redirect, (app) portals, api/v1, src/server (db, actor, scope, outbox, audit, domain), src/contracts (Zod schemas feeding OpenAPI), worker/ (pg-boss boot + outbox drain, jobs).

nodes.label: Campaign Order Acceptance (Signature Capture)
nodes.rationale: What matters legally is not a signature image — it is proof of exactly which text was shown, to whom, when, and from where. Hash the rendered agreement body at display time and store bodyHash, ip, userAgent and guardianId with the AgreementAcceptance; acceptance flips the order to ACCEPTED and creates deliverables from the job (§13 step 7). Warning: do not build this until the templates exist — the Campaign Order and Content Collaboration Agreement are missing from the operations binder; hashing text that has not been through counsel builds an audit trail for an unenforceable agreement.

nodes.label: Partial Unique Index for Single-Use Redemption
nodes.norm_label: partial unique index for single-use redemption
nodes.rationale: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX reward_single_redeem ON RewardEvent(tokenId) WHERE type='REDEEM' — one redemption per single-use token, enforced by Postgres, not application code. Two fans scanning the same code within the same millisecond is not hypothetical at an event; an application-level 'have we already redeemed?' check loses that race every time, a unique index cannot. Catch the constraint violation and render 'already used' — the correct implementation of §16's single-use rule.

nodes.label: Tenant Scoping and Authorization Pattern
nodes.rationale: Two files no query may skip: actor.ts answers who is asking (requireActor from Clerk auth to User mirror row); scope.ts answers what they may see, as a Prisma where fragment spread into every query, with DENY ({id:'__deny__'}) as the safe default. Field-level leaks are the failure mode, not row-level ones: a sponsor legitimately sees an athlete row but must not see another sponsor's AthleteRate.amount; an athlete must never see Campaign.budget. Use explicit select — never include — on every sponsor- and athlete-facing query, plus a lint rule failing the build on bare findMany() with no select.

nodes.label: Tracking and Reward Funnel
nodes.rationale: The platform's only first-party data. Four event types as four separate rows: SCAN when the QR resolves, LANDING when the page renders, CLAIM when the fan takes the offer, REDEEM when validated — §16 requires the separation and the funnel is worthless without it. Tracking redirect logs via after() so the fan never waits on the write. The redeem page must render without JavaScript: hit on a phone, on venue wifi, once — server component, no client bundle, no font that blocks paint.

nodes.label: Transactional Job Enqueue (Outbox Pattern)
nodes.rationale: The reason for Postgres queueing: an outbox row is written in the same transaction as the record that caused it — either both land or neither — so a campaign can never go live without its Zoho sync queued, and a queued sync can never point at a rolled-back campaign. Worker drains OutboxJob to pg-boss every second using FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, which is what allows two worker instances without double-processing; drop it and a second worker starts double-sending sponsor emails. Partial index outbox_pending on createdAt WHERE dispatchedAt IS NULL keeps the drain scanning only undispatched rows.

nodes.label: Zoho Sync Loop Prevention
nodes.rationale: Bi-directional sync fails in one predictable way: SponsorX writes to Zoho, Zoho's webhook fires back, SponsorX writes again. Two fields prevent it — lastSyncOrigin (SPONSORX | ZOHO) and lastSyncHash (sha256 of stable-stringified payload). If origin is ZOHO and the hash matches, the event is an echo and is dropped. External_Id carries the SponsorX id as the dedupe key per §18. Inbound webhook route verifies the Zoho signature before parsing.

nodes.label: Bundled Athlete Network Model
nodes.rationale: The two-sided problem: one athlete with 20,000 followers is not worth the hassle of a contract, but ten of them is a real campaign — with ten contracts, ten negotiations and ten people to chase; meanwhile the athlete has a real engaged audience but is too small for a brand to bother with. SponsorX sits in the middle and bundles them: many small audiences become one sellable thing, and one business deals with one invoice. The business never finds an athlete, negotiates a rate, writes a contract, or chases a deliverable.

nodes.label: Do Not Lead With Reach
nodes.rationale: The current homepage says '1.2M Monthly Reach / 2.4M Fans Engaged' — the old pitch, selling audience size, which invites comparison to buying ads, a game you lose on price. The current strategy sells outcomes: lead with '$750, three athletes, and a number you can check'.

nodes.label: Pilot Campaigns as Proof-Building
nodes.rationale: Four anchor athletes, no completed campaigns yet. The first five campaigns are not sales, they are proof-building — price them as pilots and get written permission to publish the numbers. Until then, do not imply results you do not have; the case-study slots on the homepage are deliberately empty for exactly this reason. Figures used in the explainer are illustrative, not results.

nodes.label: Redemption as Proof (The Differentiator)
nodes.rationale: Step four is the one thing that makes it different: every other form of local sponsorship ends at 'your logo was seen'; this one ends at '1,870 people used your code'. That is the whole pitch — everything else is a feature; this is the reason to believe. Answer to 'how do I know it worked?': because the offer is redeemed in your store. Not impressions. Redemptions.

nodes.label: Zoho Boundary
nodes.rationale: One sentence settles most future arguments: Zoho knows who you're selling to and whether they've paid; SponsorX knows what was promised, who's delivering it and whether it worked. Zoho is the sales system, not the platform. Three exchanges cross between them, all through the worker, all queued — if Zoho goes down, sponsors still browse, athletes still accept orders, fans still redeem; syncs just wait.

nodes.label: Branded State System (states.tsx)
nodes.rationale: Accent-shimmer skeletons mirroring real layouts, EmptyState with SVG mark + next-action link, ErrorPanel with reference code + retry; loading.tsx per route, error.tsx per group, branded 404; prefers-reduced-motion safe.

nodes.label: ?demo= State Switcher
nodes.rationale: Pages read ?demo=loading|empty|error server-side via demoState(searchParams) and render that state live — demoable to the client and real wiring for Block B; production behavior unaffected when the param is absent.

nodes.label: Frost Light Theme
nodes.rationale: [data-theme=light] re-points the same --sx-* custom properties (dark stays :root default) so both themes cascade through Tailwind's @theme inline mapping with no class changes; brand hues darkened one step for AA contrast; sun/moon toggle + localStorage + pre-paint inline script; redeem page stays dark (no-JS rule).

nodes.label: Locked Statistic Inventory (Stat → Source → Label)
nodes.rationale: Every sponsor-page statistic mapped to its retrieval source and provenance label; demographics, sentiment, real-time counters and view-through attribution are excluded because no Phase 1 retrieval path exists.

nodes.label: Platform-Split Sourcing Plan (Layers 0–4)
nodes.rationale: Layer 0 grouping is structural (MetricDaily → Deliverable → platform); Layer 1 staff-logged VERIFIED_MANUAL counts; Layer 2 sync-social-metrics worker polling YouTube Data API v3 (public, no OAuth); Layer 3 IG Graph + TikTok Display via athlete OAuth (TikTok app review is a lead-time item); Layer 4 our own t/[code] LinkEvents — platform data fully owned today. Engagement definitions normalized in the worker.

nodes.label: Provenance Chips (VERIFIED / MANUAL / ATTRIB / EST)
nodes.rationale: §22 provenance on every soft number — the provenance system is a feature, not a disclaimer.

nodes.label: A0 · Brand Retheme
nodes.rationale: Replace mockup-v1.0 purple/teal with the BTG logo's blue/orange via a token swap in globals.css — semantic tokens cascade through all ~25 routes; portal accents follow the logo; dark stays primary, light variant deferred to A2.

nodes.label: A1 · Build the 10 Remaining Stub Routes
nodes.norm_label: a1 · build the 10 remaining stub routes
nodes.rationale: Three loop-aligned batches (front door + athlete side, BTG operations, sponsor public + property); field-level rule enforced from fixtures onward — sponsor-facing screens never display AthleteRate.amount. Exit: no ScreenStub remains.

nodes.label: A2 · State & Polish Pass
nodes.rationale: Loading/empty/error states for every screen, the light-theme variant, responsive phone-to-desktop, and the redeem page verified to render without JavaScript (§16 — hit once, on venue wifi, on a phone).

nodes.label: A3 · Fixture Completeness
nodes.rationale: Extend fixtures.ts so every screen's every state is representable (minor with unverified guardian, expired invite, under-delivering campaign, held earning), keeping every shape mirroring the V2 Prisma models so Block B stays a substitution.

nodes.label: Block A — Finish the UI Scaffold (Fixtures Only)
nodes.norm_label: block a — finish the ui scaffold (fixtures only)
nodes.rationale: Everything renders on fixtures.ts / mock-auth.ts — no database, no auth, no network. Goal: a complete, on-brand, clickable demo of the entire §39 loop on mock data, so Block B is pure substitution behind finished screens.

nodes.label: Metric Provenance Labels
nodes.rationale: verified-API / verified-manual / self-reported / estimated / attributed, carried end-to-end — the mitigation for Phase 1's largely manual metrics being oversold as verified.

nodes.label: A2 State & Polish + Portal-Wide Stats Wow — Implementation Plan
nodes.norm_label: a2 state & polish + portal-wide stats wow — implementation plan
nodes.rationale: Foundation first (theme tokens + toggle, white-alpha sweep, branded state system, ?demo= switcher), then one committed vertical slice per portal (admin → athlete → property → public). All server-rendered SVG + CSS motion; only client islands are the theme toggle, CountUp and error.tsx boundaries; zero new dependencies.

nodes.label: Sponsor Portal Redesign — Implementation Plan
nodes.rationale: Nine tasks rebuilding the four sponsor pages to the approved Command Deck hero + Executive Bento design: new chart/hero primitives in charts.tsx and hero.tsx (server components, hand-rolled SVG), append-only fixture extensions, four page rewrites; verification via tsc/eslint/next build/acceptance greps since no test framework exists until B0.

nodes.label: A2 State & Polish + Portal Wow — Design Spec
nodes.norm_label: a2 state & polish + portal wow — design spec
nodes.rationale: Approved user decisions: combined A2 pass extended with sponsor-grade stats for admin/athlete/property/public; Frost light theme via data-theme toggle; branded states; differentiated per-portal heroes; foundation-first sequencing. §2 tables give every hero stat a fixture value and a Block B retrieval path.

nodes.label: Sponsor Portal Redesign — Design Spec
nodes.rationale: Client-demo wow within Phase 1 architecture: server-rendered only, every number retrievable, §22 provenance everywhere, §17 managed marketplace (never checkout), AthleteRate.amount never on sponsor pages, fixtures stay shaped to V2 Prisma models so Block B remains a substitution, mobile-first.

nodes.label: UI-Scaffold-First Strategy
nodes.rationale: The prototype is §12's step 6 (UI) built ahead on fixtures. Because the fixtures mirror the real V2 Prisma models, replacing them is a substitution, not a rewrite — which is exactly why finishing the UI scaffold before the backend is safe here.
